newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rally after Japan reassures Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally after Japan reassures Wall Street.

text.p: Stocks recovered some of the previous session's deep losses on Tuesday after Japan reassured Wall Street that it was not planning an imminent sale of its U.S. government bond holdings.
But the market's bounce was hampered by lurking inflation fears.

At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 30.76 points at 7,635.02, a day after the blue-chip index took it on the chin in a 192-point plunge on comments by Japan's prime minister about potential Japanese sales of U.S. government bonds.
It was the second-biggest setback ever in point terms for the world's most closely-watched stock index after the 508-point drop when the market crashed on Oct. 19, 1987.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 14-11 on volume of 287 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq composite index rose 4.22 points to 1,438.54.

Japan came to the market's rescue overnight, and reassured financial markets. Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said, "The prime minister's real intention was not correctly reported" and that Japan had no intention of selling U.S. Treasuries.

On Monday, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech in New York, said that Japan had been tempted in the past to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.
Wall Street viewed the comment as a veiled threat by Hashimoto to sell off Japan's U.S. Treasury holdings.
Analysts said the stock market had overreacted to Hashimoto's comments.
"The market should not have even gone down yesterday, but it's a very nervous market so it is vulnerable to almost any bad news," said James Melcher, president of Balestra Capital.
The bond market also rallied. The benchmark 30-year Treasury was up 5/32, trimming its yield to 6.69 percent from 6.70 percent on Monday.
"The tempest in the Japanese teapot has calmed down," said Alfred Kugel, Stein Roe senior investment strategist.
He said Hashimoto's comments had provided an excuse to take profits.
Analysts said the Dow's rebound lost some steam after the release of stronger-than-forecast consumer confidence data.
The Conference Board, a private business research group, said its index of U.S. consumer confidence rose to 129.6 for the month, its highest level since August 1969.
Ken Goldstein, senior economist at the Conference Board, told Reuters Financial Television that U.S. prices were not completely under control, adding he expected an uptick in inflation down the road.
Traders also said the stock market remained jittery.
"Yesterday's sell-off was significant," said Warren Epstein, director of trading at Richard Rosenblatt. "People are just more cautious."

Among individual stocks, PacifiCare Health Systems Inc. lost nearly 21 percent of its value after the company said its second-quarter earnings would fall short of analysts' estimates. Its stock was down 17-1/2 at 36-1/2.

Bristol Myers Squibb Co. rose 5-1/4 points at 81-5/8 in brisk trade. A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel voted unanimously to approve the company's paclitaxel drug as a second-line therapy for Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer affecting 20,000 AIDS patients.
International Business Machines Corp., a Dow component, was up 2-1/2 at 90-1/2. The investment firm, Morgan Stanley said it raised its price target on IBM to $105 per share from $93 per share.
